Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Human rights groups in Bangladesh and abroad are calling for an investigation after 16 borders guards accused of participating in a bloody revolt in February died in custody in recent days. A Bangladesh Rifles soldier is shown wearing a white cloth signifying surrender in late February. The Bangladesh military acknowledged the deaths of the Bangladesh Rifles paramilitary troops, or jawans -- but insisted they were the result of illness and suicide. "Given the history of abuses by security forces in Bangladesh, there is no reason to take at face value the claim that these detainees have committed suicide," said Brad Adams, Asia director or the New York-based Human Rights Watch, in a statement. The 16 were among 1,100 jawans rounded up after a 35-hour mutiny that began on February 25 in the Rifles headquarters in the capital city, Dhaka. The jawans rebelled against their commanding officers, taking dozens of them hostage. When the standoff ended, more than 70 people were found dead -- the majority of them army officers. Initially, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina promised the jawans amnesty if they laid down their arms. But once the scope of the massacre came to light, Hasina withdrew her offer -- saying the government will not show mercy to those who killed, looted or committed arson. The jawans were issued an ultimatum to turn themselves in, while the government created a committee to probe into the mutiny. The result of the government inquiry is yet to be made public, after several delays. On Thursday, the Rifles leadership issued a statement that said 16 detainees have died in custody since March 9: four from suicide, six from heart attacks and six from other diseases. "We believe that perhaps they have failed to cope with the mental pressure associated with the guilt of committing the brutal attacks,"the statement said. It then added: "Suicide is seen as a sin in religious terms and is also socially undesirable." In response, the legal aid group, Ain o Salish Kendro (Law and Adjudication Center), and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association were among several organizations calling for an investigation. During a hearing Wednesday, one of the suspects told a Dhaka court he had been administered electric shocks during a seven-day detention. Family members of other detainees have made similar allegations. Some of the suspects who died in custody had wounds on their bodies consisted with torture, Human Rights Watch said. Bangladeshi authorities have said the wounds may have been inflicted when the suspects tried to escape from the Rifles headquarters after the rebellion. "The explanations given by representatives of the security forces are simply not credible," Adams said. "Torture is a regular 'investigative technique' in Bangladesh and killing of detains in government custody is an endemic problem." The country's elite anti-crime unit, Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), have often been accused of 'extra-judicial' killings. The battalion is involved in the interrogation of many of the Rifles suspects. Since its inception in 2004, more than 550 alleged criminals died soon after they were captured by RAB forces. In each case, the battalion claimed the arrested men died from stray bullets as their units were engaged in gun battles with the suspects' comrades. The 65,000-strong Bangladesh Rifles is responsible primarily for guarding the country's borders, but it also takes part in operations such as monitoring polls. It is distinct from the army, but their commanders are career army officers. The troops staged their rebellion on the second day of BDR Week, when officers and troops from various BDR outposts along the border were in the capital for celebrations. Discontent had been bubbling for years in the ranks of the BDR, who complained their army superiors dismissed their appeals for more pay, subsidized food and their requests to participate in United Nations peacekeeping operations -- which pay far more than what they make at home. Bangladesh and its South Asian neighbors are the largest troop contributors to U.N. peacekeeping operations. During the stand-off, dozens of officers were killed. Some bodies were dumped in mass graves. Others were tossed in sewers that emptied into a river, where they floated for miles before being retrieved.

A Bangladesh Rifles soldier was shown wearing a white cloth signifying surrender in late February.

The Bangladeshi military acknowledged the deaths of the Bangladesh Rifles paramilitary troops, known as jawans, but insisted that they resulted from illness and suicide.

“Given the history of abuses by security forces in Bangladesh, there is no reason to take at face value the claim that these detainees have committed suicide,” Brad Adams, Asia director of the New York-based Human Rights Watch, said in a statement.

The 16 were among 1,100 jawans rounded up after a 35-hour mutiny that began February 25 at the Rifles headquarters in the capital, Dhaka. The jawans rebelled against their commanding officers and took dozens of them hostage.

When the standoff ended, more than 70 people were found dead, the majority of them army officers.

Initially, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina promised the jawans amnesty if they laid down their arms. But once the scale of the massacre came to light, Hasina withdrew her offer, saying the government would show no mercy to those who had killed, looted, or committed arson.

The jawans were given an ultimatum to turn themselves in, while the government established a committee to investigate the mutiny. After several delays, the findings of the government inquiry have yet to be made public.

On Thursday, the Rifles leadership issued a statement saying that 16 detainees had died in custody since March 9: four by suicide, six from heart attacks, and six from other illnesses.

“We believe that perhaps they have failed to cope with the mental pressure associated with the guilt of committing the brutal attacks,” the statement said.

It added: “Suicide is seen as a sin in religious terms and is also socially undesirable.”

In response, the legal aid group Ain o Salish Kendro (Law and Adjudication Center) and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers’ Association were among several organizations calling for an investigation.

During a hearing Wednesday, one of the suspects told a Dhaka court that he had been subjected to electric shocks during a seven-day detention. Family members of other detainees have made similar allegations.

Some of the suspects who died in custody had wounds on their bodies consistent with torture, Human Rights Watch said. Bangladeshi authorities have said the wounds may have been inflicted when the suspects attempted to escape from the Rifles headquarters after the rebellion.

“The explanations given by representatives of the security forces are simply not credible,” Adams said. “Torture is a regular ‘investigative technique’ in Bangladesh, and the killing of detainees in government custody is an endemic problem.”

Discontent had been building for years among the BDR’s ranks. Troops complained that their army superiors had dismissed their appeals for higher pay and subsidized food, as well as their requests to participate in United Nations peacekeeping operations, which pay far more than they earn at home.

Human rights organizations in Bangladesh and overseas have demanded an inquiry into the recent deaths in detention of 16 border guards suspected of involvement in February’s deadly uprising.

A photograph from late February showed a Bangladesh Rifles soldier wearing a white cloth to indicate surrender.

Bangladesh’s military confirmed that the 16 members of the Bangladesh Rifles paramilitary force—known as jawans—had died, but maintained that disease and suicide were responsible.

Brad Adams, the Asia director of New York-based Human Rights Watch, said Bangladesh’s record of misconduct by security agencies meant official assertions that the prisoners had killed themselves should not simply be accepted.

The dead men were among approximately 1,100 jawans detained following a 35-hour revolt that began on February 25 at the Rifles headquarters in Dhaka, the national capital. During the mutiny, jawans turned against their commanders and held dozens of officers hostage. After the confrontation ended, authorities discovered the bodies of more than 70 people, most of whom were army officers.

Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina initially offered amnesty to the mutineers if they surrendered their weapons. She later revoked that pledge after the extent of the killings became known, declaring that the government would show no leniency toward anyone responsible for murder, looting or arson.

The jawans were ordered to surrender by a specified deadline, and the government established a committee to investigate the rebellion. Despite repeated postponements, the committee’s findings have not yet been released publicly.

In a statement issued Thursday, the Rifles command said the 16 prisoners had died between March 9 and the date of the announcement. According to its account, four took their own lives, six suffered fatal heart attacks and another six died from various illnesses.

The statement suggested that the detainees may have been unable to withstand the psychological strain caused by guilt over the violent attacks. It also noted that suicide is religiously regarded as sinful and is socially unacceptable.

Several groups responded by pressing for an investigation, including the legal-aid organization Ain o Salish Kendro, also called the Law and Adjudication Center, and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers’ Association.

At a court hearing in Dhaka on Wednesday, one suspect said he had been subjected to electric shocks while held for seven days. Relatives of other detainees have reported comparable abuse.

Human Rights Watch said some prisoners who died bore injuries compatible with torture. Bangladeshi officials argued that the wounds might have been sustained as the suspects attempted to flee the Rifles compound after the uprising.

Adams rejected the security forces’ explanations as implausible. He said torture is routinely employed in Bangladesh as a method of investigation and that deaths of detainees in state custody are a widespread, persistent problem.

The Rapid Action Battalion, or RAB—Bangladesh’s elite crime-fighting force—has repeatedly faced allegations of extrajudicial killings. Its personnel have participated in questioning many of those accused in the Rifles rebellion.

Since RAB was created in 2004, more than 550 suspected criminals have died shortly after being taken into its custody. In every instance, the unit said the detainees were hit by stray gunfire when RAB officers became involved in shootouts with associates of the suspects.

The Bangladesh Rifles has about 65,000 personnel. Its chief duty is protecting the country’s frontiers, although it also assists with activities such as election monitoring. The force is separate from the army, but career military officers serve as its commanders.

The revolt began on the second day of BDR Week, a period of festivities that had brought officers and troops from Bangladesh Rifles border posts around the country to Dhaka.

Resentment had been building among rank-and-file BDR members for years. They said their army commanders ignored demands for higher salaries, subsidized food and opportunities to join United Nations peacekeeping missions, which provide much greater earnings than they receive domestically. Bangladesh and neighboring South Asian countries supply more troops to U.N. peacekeeping operations than any other region.

Dozens of officers were killed during the standoff. Some victims were buried in mass graves, while others were thrown into sewer channels leading to a river. Their bodies drifted for miles before they were recovered.

Human rights organizations are calling for an independent investigation into the deaths of 16 Bangladesh Rifles personnel who died in custody after being detained in connection with a bloody mutiny in February. The uprising at the border force’s headquarters in Dhaka left more than 70 people dead, including dozens of army officers, and prompted the authorities to detain large numbers of guards for questioning and prosecution.

Military officials said the 16 detainees died from causes including suicide, heart attacks, and illness. Rights advocates, however, said those explanations should not be accepted without impartial autopsies and transparent inquiries. The groups urged the government to disclose where and under what conditions the guards had been held, provide access to medical and postmortem records, and allow independent monitors to interview surviving detainees. They also called for anyone found responsible for torture or unlawful deaths to be prosecuted.

While acknowledging the seriousness of the mutiny and the need to bring those responsible for the killings to justice, advocates stressed that the investigation must comply with national and international human-rights standards. They said the government’s handling of the custody deaths would be an important test of its commitment to due process, transparency, and accountability.

### Bangladesh Through a Human Lens

CNN’s coverage of Bangladesh often highlights the human stories behind the country’s rapid transformation. Home to more than 170 million people, Bangladesh has achieved notable progress in education, public health, women’s participation in the workforce, and disaster preparedness. At the same time, its people continue to face challenges such as poverty, urban overcrowding, labor rights concerns, and the growing effects of climate change.

From garment workers in Dhaka to farmers living near flood-prone rivers, each human experience reveals both vulnerability and resilience. International media organizations like CNN can help bring these stories to a global audience, encouraging viewers to see Bangladesh not simply through statistics or headlines, but through the lives, ambitions, and dignity of its people.

counterfactuals.output:
### Rights groups seek probe into deaths of 16 Bangladesh border guards

**Dhaka, Bangladesh (CNN) —** Human rights groups have called for an independent investigation into the deaths in custody of 16 Bangladesh Rifles soldiers accused of involvement in a deadly mutiny in February.

The groups said allegations that some detainees were tortured must be examined promptly and impartially. Authorities have attributed several of the deaths to illness, heart attacks or suicide, but activists say the circumstances raise serious concerns about the treatment of suspects.

Thousands of border guards were detained after the two-day uprising at the force’s headquarters in Dhaka, where more than 70 people were killed, including dozens of army officers.

Rights advocates have urged the government to ensure detainees have access to lawyers, medical care and their families, and that any officials responsible for abuse are held accountable.

Bangladeshi authorities have said the deaths are being reviewed and have denied that torture is systematic. The government has pledged to prosecute those responsible for the mutiny through the country’s legal system.

Human rights organizations stressed that the scale and brutality of the uprising do not diminish Bangladesh’s obligation to protect people in state custody and provide all defendants with fair trials.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the controversy surrounding the deaths of detained jawans after the 2009 Bangladesh Rifles revolt, including allegations of torture, the military’s explanations, and Human Rights Watch’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
After the February 2009 Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) mutiny, dozens of detained rank-and-file soldiers—“jawans”—died while being interrogated or held in military and other government custody. Relatives, survivors, lawyers, and rights groups alleged that detainees were severely beaten, subjected to electric shocks, deprived of food or medical care, and otherwise tortured. Some families said bodies bore bruises, wounds, or other signs inconsistent with natural death.

Military and government authorities denied systematic abuse. They generally attributed the deaths to heart attacks, kidney or liver disease, other pre-existing illnesses, or suicide, arguing that many detainees were under extreme stress following the revolt. Officials also said post-mortem examinations did not establish torture in the cases they reviewed.

Human Rights Watch rejected those explanations as insufficient given the number and pattern of deaths and the consistent torture accounts. It called for prompt, independent, and transparent investigations, public release of autopsy findings, prosecution of anyone responsible, access to lawyers and doctors for detainees, and an end to coercive interrogations. HRW also warned that mass proceedings and evidence allegedly obtained under torture undermined the detainees’ right to a fair trial.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article on the aftermath of the Bangladesh Rifles mutiny in Dhaka, covering the massacre, arrests, custodial deaths, government inquiry, and alleged abuses by security forces.
counterfactuals.output:
# Bangladesh Rifles Mutiny Left a Legacy of Massacre, Mass Arrests and Abuse Allegations

**DHAKA, Bangladesh** — The two-day mutiny at the headquarters of the Bangladesh Rifles in February 2009 ended with mass graves inside a sprawling military compound, 74 people dead and the country’s security establishment shaken by one of the bloodiest episodes in its history.

The violence began on the morning of Feb. 25 at the paramilitary border force’s headquarters in Pilkhana, Dhaka, during an annual gathering of Bangladesh Rifles personnel and senior commanders. Rank-and-file soldiers turned their weapons on officers seconded from the army, seized control of the compound and held officers and family members hostage.

By the time the uprising collapsed the following day, 57 army officers were among the dead. The victims included the force’s director general, Maj. Gen. Shakil Ahmed, and members of officers’ families. Bodies were recovered from drains, shallow graves and other locations around the compound. Some victims had been shot at close range, and reports that women were assaulted added to the national outrage, though not every allegation emerging in the immediate chaos was independently substantiated.

The massacre devastated Bangladesh’s officer corps and presented an early crisis for the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, which had taken office only weeks earlier.

## Negotiations, surrender and a search for suspects

Rather than order an immediate army assault on the densely populated compound, Hasina’s government initially pursued negotiations. Officials argued that a frontal operation could have caused far more deaths among hostages, civilians and mutineers. Critics, including some military officers and victims’ relatives, later questioned whether the delay allowed perpetrators to escape and evidence to be destroyed.

The mutineers began surrendering after the government announced an amnesty for those who had participated in the rebellion but had not committed murder or other serious crimes. That promise did not shield suspects accused of killings, hostage-taking, arson or looting.

Security forces subsequently launched a nationwide manhunt. Thousands of Bangladesh Rifles members were arrested or confined for questioning as investigators attempted to distinguish those responsible for the massacre from soldiers who had joined the mutiny, remained at the compound under coercion or played lesser roles.

The scale of the detentions was extraordinary. More than 6,000 personnel were eventually prosecuted in a series of special paramilitary proceedings for offenses connected to the revolt. Hundreds more faced a separate civilian criminal case involving murder, conspiracy and other serious charges.

The Bangladesh Rifles was later reorganized and renamed Border Guard Bangladesh, an institutional break intended to restore discipline and public confidence.

## Deaths in custody raised alarm

As arrests spread, reports began to emerge that suspects were being tortured or otherwise mistreated by the police, the Rapid Action Battalion and military intelligence personnel.

Human-rights organizations documented accounts from former detainees and relatives who said prisoners were beaten, subjected to electric shocks, suspended in painful positions, deprived of sleep or threatened into making confessions. Some detainees said interrogators demanded that they identify supposed organizers or admit to roles in the killings.

The government denied that torture was official policy and said allegations would be examined. Authorities frequently attributed deaths in custody to heart attacks, liver or kidney disease and other medical conditions.

Rights groups disputed the adequacy of those explanations. Amnesty International reported in the months after the mutiny that at least 16 detained border guards had died and called for independent investigations. Human Rights Watch later said at least 47 suspects had died in custody after the revolt, with some deaths occurring in circumstances that raised serious concerns about torture and denial of medical care.

In several cases, relatives said detainees had been healthy before arrest but their bodies bore bruises or other injuries when returned to their families. Because access to detention facilities and medical records was restricted, many claims could not be independently verified.

The custodial deaths deepened concern that the state’s response was punishing large numbers of lower-ranking soldiers without adequately establishing individual responsibility.

## Government inquiries cited grievances and intelligence failures

The government established an inquiry committee to investigate the causes of the mutiny and the authorities’ response. The army conducted a separate investigation.

The inquiries examined longstanding resentment within the Bangladesh Rifles over pay, rations, promotion opportunities, participation in lucrative United Nations peacekeeping missions and the practice of placing army officers in the force’s senior command positions. Mutineers had publicly cited many of those grievances during the rebellion.

Investigators also scrutinized failures by intelligence and security agencies to detect preparations for the uprising. Questions persisted over how armed conspirators were able to strike during a gathering that brought much of the senior leadership into one place.

The government inquiry did not publicly establish that a foreign government or major political party had directed the revolt, despite widespread rumors and competing conspiracy theories. It identified institutional grievances, poor communication and intelligence shortcomings as significant factors, while acknowledging that the exact scope of planning remained difficult to determine.

Critics said the published findings were incomplete and that portions of the investigative record were not made public. The army’s own inquiry was also not fully disclosed, fueling demands from victims’ families and opposition politicians for greater transparency.

## Mass trials and due-process concerns

The legal response unfolded through two tracks.

Special courts operating under the Bangladesh Rifles law tried thousands of personnel for mutiny-related offenses. These proceedings focused largely on participation in the rebellion rather than the massacre itself. Groups of defendants were tried together, and thousands received prison terms ranging from several months to years.

A separate civilian trial dealt with murder and other grave crimes. In 2013, a Dhaka court delivered verdicts in what was described as one of the largest criminal trials in the world. Of 846 defendants, 152 were sentenced to death, 161 received life imprisonment and more than 250 were given other prison terms. More than 270 were acquitted.

Bangladesh’s High Court later upheld most, but not all, of the death sentences and other convictions. Appeals and reviews continued for years.

Human-rights groups said the enormous number of defendants, limited access to lawyers during early detention and reliance on disputed confessions undermined confidence in the process. They argued that even the scale of the atrocity could not justify torture, collective punishment or trials in which the evidence against each accused was not rigorously examined.

The authorities maintained that the trials were conducted under Bangladeshi law and were necessary to bring justice for an unprecedented attack on the state and its armed forces.

## Families on both sides sought answers

For the families of the slain officers, the revolt left a lasting sense of betrayal. Many argued that the victims had been targeted because they represented the army leadership within the border force. Relatives repeatedly demanded a complete account of the planning behind the attack, the security failures that preceded it and the government’s decision-making during the siege.

Families of detained border guards told a different story. Some said their relatives were prosecuted merely for being present at Pilkhana or for failing to resist armed mutineers. Others said detainees disappeared for days into interrogation centers before being formally produced in court.

The competing demands — accountability for a massacre on one hand and protection against arbitrary detention and torture on the other — shaped the long aftermath of the uprising.

The mutiny exposed deep divisions between army officers and the rank and file of the border force, weaknesses in intelligence coordination and the risks of responding to mass violence through equally sweeping arrests. It also left unresolved questions about who planned the killings, whether warning signs were missed and whether all those punished had been individually proven responsible.

More than a decade later, the Pilkhana massacre remains both a national trauma and a contested chapter in Bangladesh’s justice system: a case defined by the brutality of the original crime, but also by allegations that the state’s pursuit of accountability produced further abuses behind closed doors.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened to the Bangladesh Rifles troops detained after the February 25 rebellion, and why are local and international human rights organizations calling for an independent investigation?
counterfactuals.output:
After the February 25–26, 2009 Bangladesh Rifles mutiny, thousands of BDR personnel were arrested and held for interrogation or mass trial. Many detainees reported beatings, electric shocks, and other torture; dozens subsequently died in custody. Authorities generally attributed the deaths to illness, heart attacks, or suicide, while families and rights groups said bodies showed signs of abuse and that some confessions were coerced.

Bangladeshi and international human-rights organizations called for an independent investigation because the deaths occurred in security-force custody, official explanations were inconsistent or inadequately documented, autopsies and detention conditions lacked transparency, and allegations implicated agencies that could not credibly investigate themselves. They also raised broader concerns about torture, denial of legal access, coerced testimony, and due-process violations in the large-scale trials.
